title: How to Slice Fresh Herbs Thin for Flavor‑Packed Garnishes
meta_description: Learn how to thin slice fresh herbs with a mandoline for vibrant, flavor‑packed garnishes. Step‑by‑step tips, safety tricks, and the best mandoline slicer for r
html:
When you need a garnish that sings, thin sliced fresh herbs are the secret weapon. A thin sliced fresh herbs mandoline lets you turn a handful of parsley, cilantro, or basil into delicate ribbons that melt into sauces, soups, and salads. Below is a hands‑on guide that walks you through choosing the right mandoline, mastering technique, and keeping safety front‑and‑center.

Why a Mandoline Beats a Knife for Herb Slices

Even the sharpest chef’s knife will struggle to produce uniform, paper‑thin strips without a lot of wrist work. A mandoline slicer gives you:

  • Consistent thickness—usually adjustable from 1 mm to 5 mm.
  • Speed—what takes minutes with a knife is done in seconds.
  • Less fatigue—your hands stay still while the mandoline does the work.

For restaurant‑thin, even slices of veggies and fruit fast, the Mandoline Slicer offers adjustable settings and a built‑in hand guard that makes it safe enough for home cooks.

Preparing Herbs for the Thin Sliced Fresh Herbs Mandoline

Before you feed anything into the mandoline, give the herbs a quick prep:

  1. Rinse and dry: Moisture will cause the blades to stick. Pat the leaves dry with a clean kitchen towel or use a salad spinner.
  2. Trim stems: Remove any woody or thick stems. For cilantro, pull off the larger stems; for basil, keep the tender stems if you like a bit of texture.
  3. Bundle wisely: Stack a small handful (about 1‑2 cups) of leaves together. Over‑loading the slicer can jam the blades.

Once the herbs are dry and trimmed, you’re ready to slice.

Setting Up the Mandoline Slicer for Perfect Herb Ribbons

The Mandoline Slicer has a simple dial that lets you choose the slice thickness. For garnish‑level ribbons, set the blade to the thinnest setting—usually 1 mm or the "paper‑thin" option. Attach the hand guard on the side where you’ll feed the herbs; it slides over the blade and protects your fingers while giving you a firm grip.

Position the mandoline on a stable surface, preferably a cutting board with a non‑slip base. If your model has a built‑in safety lock, engage it before you begin.

Technique: How to Slice Herbs Thin and Evenly

Here’s the step‑by‑step motion that produces restaurant‑thin slices every time:

  • Grip the hand guard: Hold the guard with your fingertips curled inward. This keeps the blade out of reach.
  • Slide, don’t force: Gently push the herb bundle forward across the blade. Let the mandoline do the cutting; excessive pressure can crush the leaves.
  • Collect the ribbons: The sliced herbs will fall onto the board or into a bowl placed beneath. Use a spatula to lift them without bruising.

If you need longer ribbons, you can stack two slices side by side and cut them again at the same setting. For a decorative twist, switch to a crinkle‑cut blade (if your mandoline model includes one) and repeat the process.

Safety Tips You Can’t Skip

Even with a hand guard, a mandoline’s blade is razor sharp. Follow these habits to avoid cuts:

  • Always keep the hand guard on when slicing.
  • Never reach across the blade to retrieve food; use a small spoon or tongs.
  • When you’re done, disengage the blade lock and store the slicer with the blade covered.

Cleaning is quick: brush off any herb residue, rinse the slicer under warm water, and dry it thoroughly before putting it away.

Creative Uses for Thin Sliced Fresh Herbs

Once you’ve mastered the technique, the possibilities expand beyond garnish:

  • Herb‑infused oils: Toss thin basil ribbons into olive oil, let sit, then strain for a green‑gold drizzle.
  • Layered salads: Stack thin cilantro strips with cucumber and radish for a crunchy, herb‑forward salad.
  • Garnish for cocktails: Float a few parsley ribbons on top of a Bloody Mary for a fresh aroma.

Because the slices are so fine, they integrate flavor without adding bulk, making every bite more aromatic.

FAQ

Can I use the mandoline for frozen herbs?

It’s best to avoid frozen herbs. The blade can become brittle, and the ice will cause uneven slices. Thaw and dry herbs before slicing.

Do I need a special blade for herb slicing?

The standard straight blade on the Mandoline Slicer works perfectly for thin ribbons. If you want a wavy texture, switch to the crinkle‑cut blade that comes with most adjustable models.

How do I store the sliced herbs to keep them fresh?

Place the ribbons in a dry paper towel-lined container and cover loosely. They stay vibrant for up to 12 hours in the refrigerator.
